description_long: Congress considered a resolution to limit President Trump's authority to continue military operations against Iran. The House vote followed a similar Senate measure that had failed, and the contemporaneous report expected the House proposal to fall short. The debate tested Congress's constitutional role in decisions to use force and the War Powers Resolution's limits on unilateral presidential action. A failed measure would leave the administration's immediate course unchanged, but the vote would still show where lawmakers stood on oversight and the legal basis for the conflict. The subsequent House rejection underscored the difficulty of building support for a congressional check during an active confrontation. The episode formed part of a longer argument over whether a president can sustain military action without explicit congressional authorization. It also put pressure on legislators to explain how they would balance national security claims with Congress's responsibility to authorize and oversee war.

existing.title: Trump signs childhood-vaccine executive order and invokes autism in remarks
existing.description_short: Trump signs childhood-vaccine executive order and invokes autism in remarks
existing.description_medium: On August 10, 2026, President Donald Trump signed Executive Order 14420 revising federal childhood-vaccine recommendations, including recommending separate administration of MMR components once available and spacing immunizations across visits. In remarks at the signing, Trump said the initiative involved autism and reiterated claims linking childhood vaccination practices to autism. Major medical and scientific reviews, including a 2025-2026 WHO evidence review, found no causal relationship between vaccines and autism.

description_long: On August 10, 2026, Trump signed Executive Order 14420 changing federal childhood-vaccine recommendations. The supplied correction describes recommendations to administer MMR components separately once available and to space immunizations across visits. During the signing, Trump said the initiative involved autism and repeated claims connecting vaccination practices with the condition. The scientific assessment cited in the correction points in a different direction: a 2025–2026 World Health Organization review found that the most rigorous evidence did not support a causal association between vaccines and autism spectrum disorder. A recommendation to change a vaccination schedule is not itself proof of the causal relationship invoked to justify it. The supported issue is the use of an autism-related claim in presenting federal vaccine policy despite contrary scientific findings.
